newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya's exiled Moslem preacher comes home.
newsitem.headline: Kenya's exiled Moslem preacher comes home.

text.p: Kenya's exiled Moslem preacher and fierce critic of President Daniel arap Moi, Sheikh Khalid Balala, returned home on Saturday after two years of exile in Germany and vowed to spearhead a campaign for constitutional reforms.

Balala, greeted by hundreds of followers chanting "Moi must go. No reforms, no elections", said he would organise a 10-million-man march to force Moi to give in to growing calls for constitutional changes.
"I will spearhead a 10-million-man march on the streets of Nairobi. We would like to see peaceful change in Kenya but at the same time we are ready and willing to pay any price," Balala said.
He added: "I am speaking as a militant Kenyan, a Kenyan who loves his country."
As he spoke, hundreds of followers including opposition leaders on hand to meet him, chanted "Moi must go, No reforms, no elections".

Balala arrived aboard a Lufthansa German airlines plane at 1755 GMT a week after Moi dramatically reversed his earlier stand not to allow the fiery preacher back home after accusing him of being a Yemeni.
He returns at a time of heightened political tension in the east African country where nine people died this week in political unrest over demands for constitutional reforms Moi has refused to enact.

Moi and Kenyan immigration officials had said Balala, who has a Kenyan mother and Yemeni father, automatically gave up his Kenyan citizenship when he failed to renounce his Yemeni citizenship at the age of 21.
Kenyan attorney general Amos Wako said Moi's decision to allow Balala back home followed appeals from many quarters including the Balala family and the Moslem community.

Political analysts said Balala's return was a major boost for the country's opposition now battling Moi, aged 73 and in power for 19 years, for sweeping constitutional reforms ahead of general elections due later this year.
Balala commands a large following in Kenya's Islam-dominated coastal region.

Two weeks ago, Balala speaking from his exile base in Frankfurt, threatened to launch a wave of popular uprisings and industrial unrest in Kenya if Moi, seeking reelection this year, did not agree to step down.

Balala had also threatened to enter the east African country illegally and wage an armed struggle to bring down Moi's government, which he accuses of being an oppressive regime and likens to that of ousted Zairean dictator Mobutu Sese Seko.
Balala was refused entry on June 7. Security officers detained him as he arrived at the coastal resort of Mombasa aboard an airliner from Frankfurt and forced him to return to Germany.
He said his Kenyan passport had expired while he was in Germany but the Kenyan embassy in Bonn refused to renew it. He said he had German travel documents but remained a Kenyan citizen.
Moi must call elections in 1997 pitting his ruling Kanu party against an opposition determined to force him to enact constitutional changes to ensure an even playing field.
But Moi has ruled out reforms before the elections and this week the opposition pressure escalated into the country's worst political violence since pluralist politics returned in 1991.
On Friday, Moi said he would take decisive action against any opposition attempt to bring chaos to the country.
His remarks were in response to a warning by opposition MPs that Kenya could slide into violence
But Moi swiftly challenged the opposition to take the debate on reforms to parliament where his ruling party holds a majority.
Moi on Thursday lambasted Western nations for urging dialogue with the opposition to end the east African nation's recent bout of unrest.
